newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Shots exchanged on Korean border before Cohen visit.
newsitem.headline: Shots exchanged on Korean border before Cohen visit.

text.p: North and South Korean troops exchanged warning shots at their tense border on Thursday, shortly before U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen flew to the area, U.S. and South Korean officials said.
Southern troops on patrol within the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) fired 10 shots into the air after spotting a group of North Korean soldiers who had crossed the border line, the officials said.
"The North Korean soldiers fired back warning shots and withdrew," a Seoul military spokesman said.

The shooting in the eastern sector of the heavily-fortified DMZ took place at 9.30 a.m. (0030 GMT). About an hour later, Cohen flew by helicopter to the border village of Panmunjom, about 100 km (60 miles) west of the flashpoint.

Standing at the DMZ, set up as a buffer zone under an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War, Cohen denounced North Korea's "decaying and dying" communist system and called on Pyongyang to make peace with South Korea.
Cohen later said of the shooting incident: "It confirms that it is still a very tense, dangerous, unstable situation as far as the North Koreans are concerned. We have to be vigilant."
Pyongyang had earlier slammed Cohen for remarks he had made about troop deployments on the Korean peninsula.
Meanwhile, South Korean President Kim Young-sam urged Pyongyang to accept a proposal for peace talks made by himself and U.S. President Bill Clinton.

North Korea has said it will respond to the offer for four-nation talks, also including China, next Wednesday, exactly one year after Clinton and Kim challenged Pyongyang to finally replace the Korean truce with a permanent peace.
"I urge North Korea to respond in a sincere manner as soon as possible to the proposal," he told a meeting of the Inter-Parliamentary Union in Seoul.
Pyongyang, desperate for food to stave off looming famine, is expected to agree to come to the peace table, but with conditions attached, Seoul officials say.
To prod Pyongyang into talks, Washington and Seoul have facilitated private food shipments to North Korea and chipped in to international charities.
The military spokesman said South Korean troops broadcast warnings through loudspeakers at five or six North Koreans near the Military Demarcation Line before firing warning shots.
"There have been exchanges of fire in the past, but this was the first shooting incident at the border this year," he said.
The demarcation line runs through the middle of the four-km (2.5 mile)-wide DMZ.

Numerous violent incidents have shattered the peace along what is now the world's last Cold War frontier. The most grisly was in 1976, when North Korean soldiers axed to death two U.S. military officers pruning a tree in Panmunjom.

Cohen, winding up his first visit to the western Pacific and Asia, said after visiting the border: "I think it's inevitable that the North cannot sustain itself, that the regime will collapse in one form or another, hopefully peacefully, perhaps violently."

Pyongyang's state radio attacked comments by Cohen that virtually all of the 37,000 U.S. troops in South Korea would remain there for the forseeable future, even if the Koreas made peace and were united.
"This outrageous comment puts military pressure on us and reveals the U.S. military forces' dangerous ambition for domination of the entire Korean peninsula," the radio said.
Cohen went to Panmunjom after talks with South Korean Defence Minister Kim Dong-jin on how to respond to a new menace posed by North Korea's chronic food shortage.
Later, Cohen met president Kim and Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha to discuss beefing up joint defences against the North.
"North Korea continues to build up its military strength and conduct exercises even though its system is loosening in every sector of society amid a severe food crisis," Kim told Cohen.
Cohen told reporters he had assured Seoul leaders that "the United States commitment to South Korea's security and regional stability is unwavering during this uncertain period."

Cohen said he and his South Korean counterpart also discussed U.S. objections to the possible South Korean purchase of Russian SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles and he was assured that Seoul remained committed to "inter-operability" with U.S. weapons.
